EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Six Ghost Supercars That almost Reached Production Before Someone Pulled the Plug
42 photos
Photo: Jaguar
Traditionally speaking, most concept cars are understood by everyone to be fiction. Almost nobody who sees one for the first time expects them to ever reach a showroom, especially when it comes to flamboyant supercar concepts, and their makers don’t expect it either.
That is not exactly the case with the following vehicles, because all of them had engineering teams, and most of them even had running prototypes or even announced production numbers. In some cases, they even had expected pricing or a list of customers ready to open their wallets for a production version.
Sadly, at one point late in the process, usually someone in charge of the budget decided to abruptly end the entire program. That is how all of the following “ghost” supercars ended up in the history books. They existed physically, some even as running prototypes, but only got featured in magazines, video games or even movies, but not in the hands of actual people who would have bought them.
The Jaguar C-X75 is the most recent such case, as a little over a year after being unveiled as a concept car at the 2010 Paris Motor show, Jaguar announced that it would build 250 examples with Williams Advanced Engineering. The production version was to use an entirely different powertrain but equally as radical as the concept, and it seems that about 100 potential customers expressed interest in buying the million-dollar hybrid supercar.
Fast forward to December 2012, and Jaguar cancelled the production because of the global economic climate, albeit it had already built five working prototypes. The shell of a C-X75, this time powered by a supercharged V8, made a surprising cameo appearance a few years later in the James Bond film Spectre, where the villain played by Dave Bautista chased Bond through Rome in one of seven actual stunt cars that Jaguar and Williams had built for the movie.
You could say that a similar story happened with the Chrysler ME Four-Twelve, which was a near-production supercar concept built around a quad-turbocharged AMG V12 with 850 horsepower. That project also ended up in the bid after Chrysler backed away for cost reasons.
A lot closer to production was the first-generation Audi R8 with a twin-turbocharged V12 diesel to complement the gasoline V8 and V10, with Ferdinand Piech adamant that such a monstrosity would do wonders for the brand’s image. It too saw working prototypes built, albeit the arrival of the global financial crisis quickly made the investment implausible.
There are only a few supercar concepts that followed a similar timeline in recent decades, and what brings them together is how close each one was to actually going into production. Neither of them got the chance to truly amaze or disappoint anyone, so nobody knows how they would have been received by real customers.
The only remaining physical memory from some of them, apart from the actual concepts or prototypes that managed to be built, are the technology patents or maybe even the powertrains they previewed. They each have an important place in the automotive history books though, and they should be celebrated as “what could have been.”
Mercedes-Benz C112: Over 700 Orders For a Phantom Supercar Most cancelled supercars on this list didn’t end up in production for fear that they wouldn’t sell and/or various global economic reasons, but that is not the case with the innovative Mercedes-Benz C112 concept, unveiled to great success at the 1991 Frankfurt Motor Show. Unlike the other examples, the C112 actually received no less than 700 orders, and Mercedes-Benz still declined to build it.
The concept car was born out of Stuttgart’s incredibly successful return to sports car racing, after the Sauber-Mercedes partnership won them the Group C world championship and even the 24 Hours of Le Mans race. In fact, pretty much everyone thought that the C112 was built to celebrate that success and as a road-going counterpart to the Mercedes C11 that won the 1990 Group C championship..
Photo: Mercedes-Benz AG As an ode to the legendary 300 SL, the mid-engine supercar used upward-opening doors and, despite being styled by Bruno Sacco’s design team at Mercedes-Benz, the concept car was actually built by Carrozzeria Coggiola, in Turin. Probably following this success, Mercedes would collaborate with Coggiola on other outlandish concept cars from the 1990s and early 2000s as well.
The engine powering the C112 was the then-new 6.0-liter V12 from the S-Class, which delivered a healthy 408 PS (402 HP) and 580 Nm (428 lb-ft). Codenamed M120, versions of it would go on to power the Pagani Zonda as well, but the C112 was the first car in which it was ever paired with a six-speed manual transmission.
What surrounded that engine was a lot more impressive, and I’m not even talking about the design. In fact, the C112 was the first Mercedes-Benz to feature a version of the Active Body Control suspension system, which was still circa 8 years away from debuting in production in the CL-Class of 1999. It also had electronically controlled rear-wheel-steering, tire pressure monitoring and an early version of radar-guided cruise control.
On top of it, it also had active aerodynamics, with the front spoiler and massive but usually hidden rear wing adjusting themselves depending on speed. The rear wing could also flip up to act as an airbrake, a concept that harked back to versions of the 1950s 300 SLR, and that would only debut in production on the SLR McLaren over a decade later.
While the 4.9 seconds required to go from 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) and the 309 kph (192 mph) top speed were not exactly ground-breaking, the 998 kg (2,200 lb) of downforce at top speed was. No less than 700 people placed orders in blind for the C112 following its reveal, but Mercedes executives decided that the brand didn’t need a flagship supercar and that its success in motorsport was enough marketing.
Ford GT90: A Quad-Turbocharged V12 Ford That Never Got to Be When the GT90 appeared at Ford’s booth at the 1995 Detroit Auto Show, everyone thought it would be Detroit’s answer to the McLaren F1. Despite its name drawing a connection to the Le Mans and Ferrari-destroying GT40, its design looked like something from a Sci Fi movie, especially in that white paint, featuring a triangular exhaust outlet.
Believe it or not, the Ford GT90 had been built in secrecy by a small team in a little over 6 months, at a reported cost of about $3 million. Because at the time Jaguar was owned by Ford, engineers borrowed heavily from the XJ220, with the GT90 sitting on a lengthened version of the Jaguar’s aluminum honeycomb chassis. It also used the model’s double-wishbone suspension and five-speed manual gearbox.
Photo: Ford What it didn’t use was a Jaguar engine, despite the British company having a V12 of its own, the GT90’s powertrain was actually a one-off, with the 5.9-liter, 48-valve V12 being based on Ford’s Modular V8. With the addition of four extra cylinders and four Garrett turbochargers, power was quoted at 730 PS (720 HP) and 895 Nm (660 lb-ft) of torque.
While it was never tested, Ford argued that that power was enough for the GT90 to hit 60 mph (97 kph) in just 3,1 seconds and reach an estimated top speed of 407 kph (253 mph), or enough to beat the McLaren F1 record at the time. Its exhaust allegedly would melt the surrounding bodywork, which is why the triangular outlet was accompanied by ceramic heat shielding.
Whether as a successor to the GT40 or as a stand-alone, world-beating supercar, everyone thought that the Ford GT90 was heading into production. Sadly, Ford didn’t budge at the massive interest surrounding the model, and the car remained a one-off tour de force. It did make the rounds on every major car racing video game of the late 1990s, and it’s probably the only American car of that era to print more bedroom posters than the Viper.
Chrysler ME Four-Twelve: A Running Prototype, Not a Concept Car The early 2000s were filled with a plethora of outlandish-looking concept cars from American carmakers, and the Chrysler ME Four-Twelve made no exception. However, unlike most of the others, the unconventional-looking (for a Chrysler) supercar was a running prototype, not just a rolling concept.
Its odd name was actually a description of its specifications, with the “ME” coming from “mid-engine,” “four” was the number of turbochargers, and “twelve” was the number of cylinders. Chrysler was part of the ill-fated DaimlerChrysler conglomerate at the time, so the engine was actually developed by AMG. Oddly enough, it wasn’t a modified version of the three-valves-per-cylinder M275 from the “65 AMG” models.
Photo: Chrysler Instead, the ME Four-Twelve resurrected the M120 6.0-liter that was also used in the C112, with four-turbochargers being attached to it thanks to the work of AMG and Pagani engineers. Output was a massive 862 PS (850 HP) and a gargantuan 1,152 Nm (850 lb-ft) of torque.
The rest of the car was equally serious, with the passenger cell being a mix of carbon fiber and aluminum honeycomb, while the gearbox of a transaxle, seven-speed dual-clutch made by Ricardo. The entire car weighed only 1,310 kg (2,888 pounds), meaning that the quoted 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) was a very much believable 2.9 seconds, while its top speed was estimated at 400 kph (248 mph).
Apart from the running concept car, Chrysler made another prototype, which it let loose on Laguna Seca at the hands of journalists, but with a detuned version of the engine. At the time, people were expecting it to enter production in 2006, but something along the way went wrong. Allegedly, Mercedes didn’t like that Chrysler would have a more powerful supercar than their own SLR McLaren, but the most probable motive was that Chrysler simply didn’t want to invest hundreds of millions in such a project without the reassurance that it would also make money.
Acura Advanced Sports Car Concept: The Lexus LFA Rival That Never Was Not long after the original NSX went out of production in 2005, Honda and Acura made no secret of wanting to replace it, and the first hint of a successor appeared at the 2007 Detroit Auto Show. Unlike its RWD, V6-powered, mid-engine predecessor, the Acura Advanced Sports Car Concept was a front-engined coupe with a naturally aspirated V10 with all-wheel-drive.
In short, it turned the original formula around, and people didn’t seem to mind it. That said, the show car itself was a non-running model, with the technical details actually coming from Honda executives after it was unveiled. They confirmed the V10 and SH-AWD system, with report putting the powertrain’s displacement at around 5.0-liter, while its output was expected to be in the 500 to 600 HP ballpark.
Photo: Acura In short, Honda was working on a direct rival to both the Nissan GT-R R35 and the Lexus LFA. Initially, the ASCC’s design received a lukewarm response, so Honda apparently sent it back to the drawing board several times before announcing that the NSX’s replacement would be launched sometime in 2010.
For over a year, engineering was in full throttle, with several camouflaged prototypes being tested at the Nurburgring Nordschleife, where the new NSX was supposed to beat the Nissan GT-R’s time. Unfortunately, the 2008 world financial crisis reached Japan as well, and Honda was forced to announce that the V10-powered NSX successor would halt development, coinciding with the carmaker’s exit from Formula 1 as well.
Those camouflaged prototypes did get an unusual afterlife though, with the HSV-010 GT competing in Japan’s super GT series between 2010 and 2013 using them as base, despite the road car having been canceled. It remains one of the very few racing cars derived from a production model that was never produced.
Audi R8 V12 TDI: The Diesel Supercar That Would Have Changed Everything Oddly enough, a diesel-powered supercar seemed like a reasonable idea back in 2008, especially for Audi, which had won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in both 2006 and 2007 using the devil’s fuel. On top of it, back then diesel was the king of European car sales, so putting the two together looked like the obvious step for the Ingolstadt carmaker.
As one of Ferdinand Piech’s babies, as he was the one who pushed the most for its existence, the Audi R8 V12 TDI was unveiled at the 2008 Detroit Auto Show. Instead of the gasoline V8 or V10 from the regular R8, behind the seats sat a 6.0-liter, twin-turbocharged V12 diesel, which delivered 500 PS (493 HP) and a massive 1,000 nm (738 lb-ft) of torque.
Photo: Audi AG Even crazier was that all that oomph was delivered to all four wheels through a six-speed manual transmission instead of a double-clutch or an automatic. Audi quoted 4.2 seconds to 100 kph (62 mph) and a top speed of more than 300 kph (186 mph), making the diesel just a tad quicker than the V8-powered, gasoline version.
That said, the car had a lot of issues with packaging, as the V12 diesel was not only much larger than the V8, but also made the car about 300 kg (661 pounds) heavier. It also needed far more cooling, so the vents grew by some 20 percent, and a NACA duct was cut into the roof to feed air to the intercoolers.
Even the suspension and brakes were reworked to handle the extra weight, and all these changes were definitely quite manageable on what was essentially a show car. What was not manageable was lifting all those modifications to series production standards, which is why Audi announced that the cost of re-engineering the R8 around such a massive engine was simply too great for recouping the investment from sales, especially since the financial crisis was in full swing at the time.
Jaguar C-X75: The One That Almost Made It Surprisingly, no car on this list got further than the Jaguar C-X75 on the way to production. The British carmaker even put a price on it and hired a Formula 1 team to engineer it, going as far as even building five working prototypes before cancelling it.
The original concept appeared at the 2010 Paris Motor Show, and, as its name suggested, it was built to mark Jaguar’s 75th anniversary. What was unusual about it was its choice of powertrain, with the model being powered by four YASA electric motors before they were cool, with two small gas turbines acting as generators.
Photo: Jaguar A year later, it was confirmed to go into production, with Jaguar planning to build 250 of them in collaboration with Williams Advanced Engineering, and start of sales was set for 2013. The Range-extending electric powertrain from the concept was replaced with an equally innovative powertrain.
This time, the production version was supposed to be powered by a 1.6-liter four-cylinder that was both supercharged and turbocharged, and which could rev to 10,000 rpm. The engine delivered 509 PS (502 HP) on its own, but was augmented by two more YASA electric motors for a combined output of 862 PS (850 HP) and 1,000 Nm (738 lb-ft) of torque. The prototypes apparently reached 322 kph (200 mph) in testing, with a theoretical maximum speed of 354 kph (220 mph).
When all was said and done, around 100 potential customers expressed interest in buying one, and this was likely not enough to persuade Jaguar executives to forget how much it tried to sell every unit of the unsuccessful XJ220. At the end of 2012, the carmaker announced that the global economic climate wasn’t exactly friendly to launching a million dollar supercar, so the project was canceled.
